object.medium: Rag for solo piano; printed sheet music
object.description: Scott Joplin, the son of a formerly enslaved railway labourer, was playing piano in the Maple Leaf Club in Sedalia, Missouri, when the local music dealer John Stark published his 'Maple Leaf Rag' in September 1899. Joplin's contract gave him a royalty of one cent a copy, unusual for a Black composer at the time, and the piece went on to sell hundreds of thousands of copies, the first instrumental sheet music to do so. Its four sixteen-bar strains, with a syncopated right hand bouncing over a steady marching left hand, became the pattern for classic ragtime and the first distinctly American popular music to spread around the world. The cover shown is the 1899 Sedalia first edition. The visitor hears the United States Marine Band's 1906 recording, among the earliest ever made of the piece, which as a pre-1926 federal recording is in the public domain.
facts: Joplin's royalty contract with Stark, signed on 10 August 1899, is one of the earliest surviving royalty agreements for a Black American composer.
Joplin himself recorded the rag on piano rolls in 1916, a year before his death, when illness had already affected his playing.
The rag was published in Sedalia; Stark moved his firm to St. Louis the next year as sales took off.
